text: On a barren hill above Toktong Pass a single company had been holding out for five days. Fox Company of the Second Battalion Seventh Marines. Around two hundred forty men under Captain William Barber. Their job was to keep the pass open. On the very first night the Chinese surrounded them. The attacks came night after night. The Marines held a small ring of foxholes on the slope. Planes dropped ammunition and food. Some bundles landed among the enemy. Men crawled out under fire to drag back the rest. Barber was shot in the leg on the second day. He refused to be relieved. He was carried on a stretcher from position to position to direct the defense. By the end most of the company had been killed or wounded or crippled by frostbite. But Fox Hill never fell. The men at Yudam-ni knew that if the pass fell they would never make it out. So Lieutenant Colonel Raymond Davis was given a desperate task. He would take the First Battalion Seventh Marines off the road entirely. They would march cross-country at night over the mountains and reach Fox Company from behind. On the night of December first Davis led his men into the dark. Snow lay knee-deep and deeper. The temperature sank far below zero. There was no trail. Some men dozed off on their feet and had to be shaken awake. The battalion steered by the stars and fought small battles along the ridgelines. On the morning of December second they reached Fox Hill. The survivors of Fox Company came out to meet them. Both Barber and Davis would later receive the Medal of Honor. Down on the road the main column ground forward. Infantry cleared the ridges on both sides while trucks and artillery crawled along between them. Every hill had to be taken. Every roadblock had to be broken. Marine Corsair fighters flew so close overhead that spent shell casings rained down on the troops below. It took the column nearly eighty hours to cover those fourteen miles. On the evening of December third the lead elements marched down into Hagaru-ri. Behind them came the wounded and the frostbitten and the guns. Witnesses remembered that some of the men were singing the Marines' Hymn as they came in. The division was together again. Almost. From the east the news was grim. Task Force Faith had been destroyed. Of roughly three thousand Army soldiers only about a thousand reached Marine lines alive. Many of them had crawled across the frozen surface of the reservoir. But Hagaru-ri was only a stopping point. Koto-ri lay eleven more miles to the south. And the Chinese were waiting there too.
